description: Groupe d'amis passionnés d'espace et de sciences, étudiants en ingénierie et en technologies, nous participons au Space Apps Challenge pour transformer notre curiosité en projet concret, au service de problématiques spatiales réelles.
summary: NASA's first Moon Base payloads are headed for the Shackleton-de Gerlache Connecting Ridge near the lunar south pole. Before hardware flies, teams rehearse on Earth, but how lunar is a terrestrial analog, measurably? We computed the same quantities, with the same code and the same distances in metres, on the ridge (NASA LRO LOLA and Diviner data) and on Earth (ESA Copernicus 30 m terrain, NASA POWER climate): slope, multi-scale roughness and its scaling exponent, sunlit fraction and cold. Screening 84,614 land cells and measuring terrain at 180 sites, we found two measurable limits. No Earth site reaches both the roughness amplitude and the roughness exponent of the ridge (0 of 180), and no Earth site has permanently shadowed ground (0 of 15). The lunar analogs most often used are 3 to 5 times too smooth at the 60 m scale. We publish every score, the places where the analogy breaks, and a recovery test (AUC 0.779) that does not yet meet our own 0.80 pass mark, so our three candidate sites are presented as leads for field validation, not as conclusions.
details:
What it does

Teams test rovers, instruments and crew procedures on Earth before going to the Moon. But these test sites are often chosen because they look lunar, or because they are easy to reach. We wanted to measure how lunar a place on Earth really is, instead of judging by eye. Our project gives a score for each dimension, for one precise target: the Shackleton-de Gerlache Connecting Ridge, where NASA's Moon Base begins.

How it works

We measure the same quantities on the Moon and on Earth, with the same code and the same distances in metres. For the terrain, we use the median slope, the roughness ν(L) at 60, 120, 240, 480 and 960 m, and the exponent H, which says how fast roughness grows with distance (Rosenburg et al. 2011).

The lunar target comes from the LOLA 20 m polar elevation model. We take the median of 25 windows of 10.24 km on and around the ridge, and the spread between these windows gives the tolerance of each dimension. For Earth we use the Copernicus GLO-30 model, in windows of the same size. Illumination is computed from horizon angles and the position of the Sun. Cold is scored in "toward" mode: Earth can get closer to lunar temperatures but never reaches them.

We combine the dimensions into one fidelity score per site. In the recovery test we use a weighted geometric mean, so that a failure on one dimension is not hidden by a good result on another. We also check it against an arithmetic mean. Gravity, vacuum, radiation, space weathering and the length of the lunar day are not scored. For each site we list them with the facility that can test them.

Validation

We tested whether our method ranks 16 recognised analog sites above 69 random land windows. The recovery AUC is 0.779 (0.776 with an arithmetic mean). This is below the 0.80 pass mark that we fixed before the test, so we report it as a negative result.

Two other checks support the comparison. A score based only on climate performs at chance (AUC 0.514), which is why we match measured lunar targets instead of rewarding "coldest and driest". And if we degrade the same lunar terrain from 20 m to 30 m, H changes by 0.0019, well inside its tolerance of 0.015. One limit: most recognised analogs are Mars analogs, so the test measures "being a known analog" more than "looking like the lunar polar ridge".

Results

Break 1, terrain. The ridge has large relief but is smooth at short range (H = 0.959). Among 180 Earth sites, none is within 2σ of the ridge on both roughness amplitude and exponent. The closest is Mauna Kea, at 2.31σ. In the top quartile of roughness, the median exponent is 0.73. On the Moon, impacts build the large forms and regolith smooths the small scales. On Earth, water, frost and vegetation add detail at every scale at the same time.

Break 2, lighting. At the ridge the Sun never goes higher than 2.0° above the horizon, so the terrain decides the lighting. According to the LOLA illumination maps (Mazarico et al. 2011), the best point of the ridge is lit 88 % of the time, and 4.3 % of the area is never lit. On Earth, none of 15 sites has a permanently shadowed point, and the best-lit point reaches 67 %. Earth's tilt (23.44°) moves the Sun too much for both extremes to exist together.

Classic analogs. At the 60 m scale, Ries crater, Holuhraun (Iceland), Meteor Crater, Lonar and Craters of the Moon are 3 to 5 times smoother than the ridge.

Candidates for field validation. Puna de Atacama, Argentina (score 0.169): slope and kilometre-scale roughness close to the ridge, but already used for planetary science and astrobiology. Esmeralda County, Nevada (0.141): slope within 0.2° of the ridge, but the kilometre-scale relief is too weak. Prince Charles Mountains, East Antarctica (0.135): high roughness exponent, cold and dry, mapped deep-crust metagabbro, 2,558 km from the nearest known analog, but too flat. No candidate reaches our weight-stability threshold of 0.70, so they are leads, not conclusions.

Benefits and intended impact

Each fidelity card shows a test team which objectives a site can close, and which ones must go to a chamber or to flight. Rover teams preparing for the Moon Base (Lunar Terrain Vehicle Services) can see that roughness at the 60 m scale on the classic analog fields is much lower than on the ridge. Teams working on navigation in grazing light learn that no Earth site gives a Sun held at 2°, so long-shadow tests need artificial lighting. The map and all the tables are open, and can be reused for other lunar targets.

Limitations

Our horizon calculation stops at 5 km, which overestimates the lunar illumination. For this reason we use the LOLA maps as the lunar reference. The Copernicus model includes vegetation and buildings, so we restrict the scan to cold, arid cells with little vegetation. The coordinates of the known analogs are approximate (±0.5°). We describe the surface composition but do not score it: the 8 µm emission peak measured by Diviner is mostly below the shortest thermal band of ASTER, and our ASTER silica index could not separate mapped rock types, so we withdrew it. We have not done any field validation.

Tools

Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, rasterio, Matplotlib, Folium, Shapely), Leaflet for the interactive map, Google Drive for hosting.

What's next

Extend the horizon calculation to about 100 km on the lunar side, add a Mars target with the same method, and check the Prince Charles Mountains and Nevada candidates with field data or high-resolution data.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

We used Anthropic's Claude a lot. It wrote and debugged most of the Python code, searched and read the data documentation, ran the analyses we specified, and drafted and edited the English text and the figures. The team chose the angle of the challenge and the lunar target, set the requirements and the decision rules (including the 0.80 pass mark), reviewed the results and the text, and made the final decisions. Every number we computed comes from the code in our project folder applied to the cited datasets. Values taken from the literature, such as the LOLA illumination figures, are cited as such. No image, video or audio generation model was used. Our figures, maps and screenshots are drawn by SI-assisted code from the data, so each one has a visible "SI-assisted" watermark and SI metadata. Details file by file: SI_DECLARATION.md and SI_METADATA.json in the project folder.
